specAnchors.text: be able to define the terms: i standard enthalpy change of atomisation, ∆ at H ii electron affinity iii lattice energy (as the exothermic process for the formation of one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions)

primer.text: Born-Haber cycles are built from four enthalpy vocabulary items. Lattice energy forms one mole of ionic solid from gaseous ions and is strongly exothermic; atomisation makes one mole of gaseous atoms and is always endothermic; electron affinity adds an electron to a gaseous atom. This note writes the defining equations for each, including doubled and halved cases.

modules.title: Lattice energy and atomisation
modules.opening: Two definitions anchor every Born-Haber cycle. Lattice energy forms one mole of ionic solid from gaseous ions - hugely exothermic, since the lattice's electrostatic attractions lock away enormous energy. Atomisation makes one mole of gaseous atoms from an element - always endothermic, whatever the element's starting state.
keyPoints: Lattice energy (delta latt H) as a formation process: the enthalpy change when 1 mole of ionic compound is made from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.

Lattice energy is strongly exothermic, because combining gaseous ions into a lattice releases enormous electrostatic energy; the large negative value shows the ionic solid is far more stable than its gaseous ions, and the more exothermic the value, the stronger the ionic bonding.
Lattice energy cannot be measured in one direct experiment; energy cycles combine multiple values instead.
For sodium chloride the equation is Na+ (g) plus Cl- (g) forming NaCl (s), with delta latt H = -776 kJ mol^-1.
Standard enthalpy change of atomisation (delta at H) forms 1 mole of gaseous atoms from the element under standard conditions, and is always endothermic.
Sodium's atomisation is Na (s) forming Na (g) with delta at H = +108 kJ mol^-1; chlorine's is half Cl2 (g) forming Cl (g) at +121 kJ mol^-1.

low.restatement: Lattice energy: gaseous ions to solid, very negative. Atomisation: element to gaseous atoms, always positive; cycles combine them because no single experiment measures lattice energy.
low.analogy: Clapping magnets together releases a snap of energy (lattice formation); pulling a Lego brick apart costs effort (atomisation).
low.examPointer: Write state symbols (g) and (s) in every definition equation - they carry marks.

medium.restatement: The lattice is an energy vault: gaseous ions carry their charges at high potential energy, and formation locks them low. Atomisation is the entry fee paid before any ion can exist.
medium.analogy: Parking a car: rolling downhill into a secure garage (lattice) after paying at the entrance booth (atomisation).
medium.examPointer: The '-776' style value belongs to formation lattice energy - quote the direction of the equation to justify the sign.

modules.title: Electron affinity and its second step
modules.opening: Electron affinity pays the gaseous ion's bill. The first affinity - one mole of electrons joining one mole of gaseous atoms - is exothermic, as chlorine's -364 kJ mol^-1 shows. The second affinity fights repulsion: forcing an electron onto an already negative ion costs energy, so oxygen's second affinity sits at +844 kJ mol^-1.
keyPoints: Electron affinity (delta ea H): the energy change when 1 mole of electrons is taken up by 1 mole of gaseous atoms, making 1 mole of gaseous ions.
Chlorine's first electron affinity: Cl (g) plus e- forming Cl- (g), with delta ea H = -364 kJ mol^-1.
First electron affinities are exothermic, since electrons are attracted to the neutral atoms.
Second electron affinities can be endothermic: oxygen's second affinity O- plus e- forming O2- costs +844 kJ mol^-1.
The endothermic second step pays to overcome the repulsion between the negative ion and the incoming electron.

low.restatement: First electron affinity: exothermic (attraction to a neutral atom). Second: endothermic (repulsion from a negative ion), like oxygen's +844.
low.analogy: The first friend joins a picnic gladly; the second friend must push past the first to sit down, and pushing costs energy.
low.examPointer: Name repulsion as the reason for the positive second affinity - the one-word answer carries the mark.

medium.restatement: Charge is the whole story: a neutral atom welcomes the electron, an anion pushes it away, so the same process flips sign on the second step.
medium.analogy: A parking lot with free spaces (neutral) versus a full lot with an attendant pushing cars closer (negative ion).
medium.examPointer: Born-Haber cycles for 2- ions must include both affinities, one negative and one positive.

glossary.definition: The enthalpy change forming 1 mole of ionic solid from its gaseous ions; strongly exothermic.
The enthalpy change forming 1 mole of gaseous atoms from the element; always endothermic.
The energy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms gains 1 mole of electrons to form gaseous ions.
